transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Redwood SE), David Kim (Arcadia CTO), Maya Lopez (Arcadia Head of Eng), Ravi Shah (Arcadia Quant), Sophie Zhang (Arcadia Infra)

Summary (auto):
Arcadia is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a high-volume quant research assistant. Main focus was unit economics (per-token), latency SLOs, batching and KV/prefix caching impact, and budget constraints across dev->prod. Agreed next steps: pricing spreadsheet, POC scoping, sample prompts.

Topics: cost per token, batching/caching levers, quantization tradeoffs, dedicated capacity pricing, private deployment considerations, compliance notes (SOC2/KMS).

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan Miles: Hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we got most folks. Quick intros, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this.
[00:10] David Kim: Hi Jordan, David here, CTO at Arcadia, i'm joined by Maya, Ravi, Sophie.
[00:15] Maya Lopez: hey all.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood SE team, i'll drive the technical bits today.
[00:25] Ravi Shah: Ravi, quant team -- mostly going to ask about token costs and latency.
[00:30] Jordan Miles: Great, high level goal for this call is to understand your workload, budget targets, and what tradeoffs you want between latency and cost, especially since you're doing heavy sample generation for backtests.
[00:40] Maya Lopez: Yes, we're running nightly simulations, about 150M tokens per month right now, but that could double if the new model goes live. We're sensitive to per-token cost but also need sub-200ms on tail latency for interactive tooling.
[00:55] Priya Nair: Helpful. Can you clarify the interactive path vs batch? Are the 150M tokens mostly async batch runs or live interactive queries?
[01:05] David Kim: It's mixed, roughly 70% batch backtesting and 30% interactive research queries, the interactive ones need lower latency.
[01:15] Priya Nair: Perfect. So typical levers we discuss: 1) choose hosted vs dedicated vs private, 2) batching and async workers for batch workloads, 3) KV/prefix caching for repeated context, 4) model quantization or smaller model variants. All of these change the unit cost.
[01:30] Sophie Zhang: On private deployment, our security team will want KMS and audit logs, and we may prefer VPC or on-prem for data residency. But first we need a good handle on what the unit economics look like.
[01:40] Jordan Miles: Totally, we can show cost scenarios. Quick callout, hosted is fastest to start and has per-token pricing; dedicated is reserved GPU pools and gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost when you commit; private adds infrastructure overhead but gives control for compliance.
[01:55] Ravi Shah: Can you quantify per-token numbers? I know every provider gives a range, but we need apples-to-apples with our current cloud costs.
[02:05] Priya Nair: Sure, i'll summarize rough starter numbers (note: approximate, we will send a spreadsheet). Hosted for a medium-sized open model we typically show $0.0008 - $0.002 per input token depending on model/quantization and host tier. Generations (output tokens) can be similar order, so combined roundtrip varies.
[02:25] David Kim: That's a big range. How much does batching move that?
[02:30] Priya Nair: Batching can move the effective per-token compute cost significantly for batch workloads. For example, with continuous batching and a GPU-optimized runtime, you might see 20-50% reduction in per-token compute cost for large batch jobs. For latency-sensitive interactive queries batching is limited because you have to meet tail SLOs.
[02:50] Jordan Miles: Also the KV cache / prefix cache helps a lot when you have repeated context or long dialogues. If you can cache the KV state for common prefixes, you avoid recomputing from tokens which reduces token compute by up to ~30% in some workloads. But this is workload dependent.
[03:05] Maya Lopez: Can Redwood's runtime do automatic prefix caching or is that manual?
[03:10] Priya Nair: We have automatic prefix/KV caching and suggestions in Redwood Optimize. For Dedicated/private you can tune cache policies and TTLs; hosted has reasonable defaults.
[03:20] Ravi Shah: What's the tradeoff with quantization? Do we lose quality badly?
[03:25] Priya Nair: Quantization reduces model memory and can lower per-token cost by enabling smaller GPU footprints or higher packing. 4-bit Q and FP16 mixed swaps give big savings. There's some quality drop on certain tasks; we recommend evals on your prompt sets. We can run quantized vs FP16 benchmarks in the POC.
[03:40] Sophie Zhang: For budgeting: in dedicated, what's typical commit levels and how predictable are overages?
[03:45] Jordan Miles: Dedicated is committed capacity, e.g., N GPUs reserved monthly. You get predictable throughput and lower effective per-token price when utilization is high. We also offer burst capacity for short spikes. Overages can be billed at a pre-agreed rate; we can model utilization scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[04:00] David Kim: Could you show an example scenario? Like if we run 150M tokens monthly and choose dedicated with 10 GPUs vs hosted?
[04:10] Priya Nair: Yes, in our sheet we'll show three scenarios: hosted (no commit), dedicated (reserve), and private (customer-managed infra). For 150M tokens, depending on model and batching, dedicated often becomes cost-effective beyond a threshold — typically when sustained monthly tokens exceed ~80-120M, but this depends on model size and latency constraints. With your 30% interactive mix, we would split workloads to maximize batching on the batch side and route interactives to low-latency nodes.
[04:35] Ravi Shah: Are there tooling or routing rules to split requests by latency needs automatically?
[04:40] Priya Nair: Yes, Smart routing lets you route by policy e.g., latency SLO vs cost. You can designate tiers: interactive routes go to low-latency pool, batch goes to a high-throughput cost-optimized pool.
[04:55] Maya Lopez: About the per-token metric: does Redwood include tokenization differences (e.g., we use BPE vs other tokenizers)? We need the cost per semantic token not just byte tokens.
[05:05] Priya Nair: We bill on model input and model output tokens as measured by the model tokenizer. We'll include tokenizer notes in the spreadsheet and can run a tokenization pass on your sample prompts so you have an accurate estimate.
[05:20] Jordan Miles: Also worth noting caching can change the measured billed tokens vs compute tokens. If you do KV caching you'll avoid compute for cached prefixes but billing still reflects the actual request tokens unless we apply cached-response optimizations — we can explain exact billing semantics in the doc.
[05:35] Ravi Shah: Any hidden things we should account for — storage, logging, tracing, long-term retention?
[05:40] Evan Brooks: Good question. Audit logs, extended observability retention, and long-term eval storage are add-ons. Basic logs/audit are included in Dedicated/Private but retention beyond X days is an extra. We'll call this out in the TCO.
[05:55] David Kim: For POC, we want you to run a 10k prompt benchmark that reflects our nightly backtests and interactive queries. Can Redwood run this and show latency percentiles and per-token cost projections?
[06:05] Priya Nair: Yes we do benchmark runs. We'll need the prompt set, and to agree on model variants (FP16, 4-bit quant). We'll run hosted and dedicated-config benchmarks — for dedicated we'll simulate the reserved capacity sizing.
[06:20] Maya Lopez: Security quick note: SOC2, SAML/SSO, KMS support — do you support customer-managed keys in dedicated/private?
[06:25] Jordan Miles: Yes customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) are supported in Private and Dedicated with enterprise options. We'll attach the security pack and SOC2 report.
[06:35] Ravi Shah: Any pitfalls when comparing to our current self-hosted stack? We run on spot instances; pricing varies.
[06:40] Priya Nair: Spot can be cheap but comes with preemption risk and operational overhead. Redwood Dedicated offers SLA and lower ops overhead — in cost models we include ops cost savings. We'll show a blended TCO vs self-hosted.
[06:55] David Kim: Pricing model clarity is crucial — we need a clear per-token model and sensitivity analysis for quantization and caching.
[07:00] Jordan Miles: Agreed. We'll send a spreadsheet with per-token rows: model variant, quantization, batching assumption, cache hit rate scenarios, and output: estimated monthly cost, effective per-token cost, and latency percentiles.
[07:15] Maya Lopez: On timeline, we are hoping to pick a vendor by end of March and start a POC in April if the numbers look good.
[07:22] Jordan Miles: That lines up. We'll get the pricing sheet to you by Monday, Priya will setup the POC scoping next week.
[07:30] Sophie Zhang: One last thing — do you have any benchmarks for tail latency with small prompt sizes?
[07:35] Priya Nair: Yes, we have internal tail latency numbers and we'll share model-specific percentiles. For interactive small prompts you can often get median sub-100ms on optimized infra, tail depends on queueing and GC in runtime — we'll include p50/p95/p99 in the benchmark report.
[07:50] Ravi Shah: Cool. Also, can you show the math on how batching reduces cost? Even a rough formula or example would help our finance team.
[07:58] Jordan Miles: We'll include worked examples: e.g., single-request compute cost = base_cost_per_token * tokens. With batching you amortize kernel startup and increase utilization so effective per-token = base_cost_per_token * (1 - batching_savings). We'll populate numbers.
[08:10] David Kim: Anything else from Redwood?
[08:12] Evan Brooks: just to say we'll include the security docs and propose two POC windows next week.
[08:18] Maya Lopez: thanks, this was helpful.
[08:20] Jordan Miles: Great, quick recap: Jordan sends pricing & cost model by 2026-03-09; Priya proposes POC scoping times and template by 2026-03-10; Arcadia shares prompt set/volumes by 2026-03-12. We'll aim to run the initial benchmark within two weeks of getting prompts.
[08:35] David Kim: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:38] Jordan Miles: Thanks all, we'll follow up in the CRM and send calendar invites for the scoping session.

End of transcript.
